title: Which Motor Neuron, and a Recipe

scenes.tts: The same code built a motor neuron in your neck, and one in your lower back. What tells them apart?
scenes.visual: Title card: Which Motor Neuron, and a Recipe. A side view of the spinal cord, coloured by level: cervical, brachial, thoracic, lumbar.
scenes.narration: The same code built a motor neuron in your neck, and one in your lower back. What tells them apart?

scenes.tts: Position along the cord, written in Hox proteins.
scenes.visual: Hox stripes appear along the side view of the cord, a different colour at each level.
scenes.narration: Position along the cord, written in Hox proteins.

scenes.tts: Motor neurons sort into columns. The medial column drives back muscles. The lateral column, at limb levels, drives limb muscles.
scenes.visual: A cross-section at limb level: medial motor column (MMC) to axial muscles of the back; lateral motor column (LMC) to limb muscles.
scenes.narration: Motor neurons sort into columns. The medial column drives back muscles. The lateral column, at limb levels, drives limb muscles.

scenes.tts: The preganglionic column projects to autonomic ganglia.
scenes.visual: A thoracic cross-section: preganglionic column (PGC) to an autonomic ganglion. Then one LMC pool highlighted, projecting to one muscle.
scenes.narration: The preganglionic column projects to autonomic ganglia.

scenes.tts: Hox proteins act inside each cell, as repressors and activators. Hox C six, at forelimb levels, and Hox C nine, at thoracic levels, repress each other.
scenes.caption: Hox proteins act inside each cell, as repressors and activators. Hoxc6, at forelimb levels, and Hoxc9, at thoracic levels, repress each other.
scenes.visual: Two Hox proteins on the side view: Hoxc6 at brachial levels, Hoxc9 at thoracic levels, with blunt arrows pointing at each other. Credit: Dasen, Liu and Jessell, 2003.
scenes.narration: Hox proteins act inside each cell, as repressors and activators. Hoxc6, at forelimb levels, and Hoxc9, at thoracic levels, repress each other.

scenes.tts: Predict. In chick, put Hox C nine into forelimb level progenitors, and so into the motor neurons they make. What column do they become?
scenes.caption: Predict. In chick, put Hoxc9 into forelimb-level progenitors, and so into the motor neurons they make. What column do they become?
scenes.visual: On the electroporated side, brachial progenitors and the motor neurons they make carry Hoxc9 (green). Question: which column?
scenes.narration: Predict. In chick, put Hoxc9 into forelimb-level progenitors, and so into the motor neurons they make. What column do they become?

scenes.tts: Their lateral column identity is suppressed. They take on a preganglionic identity, from a thoracic column.
scenes.visual: The LMC label fades on the electroporated side; a PGC label (column of Terni, in chick) appears.
scenes.narration: Their lateral column identity is suppressed. They take on a preganglionic identity, from a thoracic column.

scenes.tts: Timing matters. Hox C nine given only after the last division suppresses the lateral column, but does not make preganglionic cells.
scenes.caption: Timing matters. Hoxc9 given only after the last division suppresses the lateral column, but does not make preganglionic cells.
scenes.visual: A second panel: Hoxc9 added only to postmitotic motor neurons. The LMC label fades; no PGC label appears. Label: CT identity needs Hoxc9 in progenitors too. Credit: Dasen, Liu and Jessell, 2003.
scenes.narration: Timing matters. Hoxc9 given only after the last division suppresses the lateral column, but does not make preganglionic cells.

scenes.tts: Hox proteins work with an accessory factor, Fox P one. It gates the limb and autonomic columns.
scenes.caption: Hox proteins work with an accessory factor, FoxP1. It gates the limb and autonomic columns.
scenes.visual: FoxP1 appears as a gate in front of the LMC (high) and the PGC (low). The MMC and HMC have no gate. Credit: Dasen et al., 2008; Rousso et al., 2008.
scenes.narration: Hox proteins work with an accessory factor, FoxP1. It gates the limb and autonomic columns.

scenes.tts: Predict. Delete Fox P one in a mouse. Are limb level motor neurons still made?
scenes.caption: Predict. Delete Foxp1 in a mouse. Are limb-level motor neurons still made?
scenes.visual: A mouse limb-level cord section with Foxp1 crossed out. Question: made?
scenes.narration: Predict. Delete Foxp1 in a mouse. Are limb-level motor neurons still made?

scenes.tts: Yes. Motor neurons are still made. What fails is the assignment of which one each is.
scenes.visual: Motor neurons fill the section, all in one plain colour. Label: made, but not assigned.
scenes.narration: Yes. Motor neurons are still made. What fails is the assignment of which one each is.

scenes.tts: They resemble the thoracic hypaxial column. In the limb, their axons appear to choose paths and muscles at random.
scenes.visual: The cells take the hypaxial-column colour. Their axons enter the limb and branch to muscles in a scrambled pattern.
scenes.narration: They resemble the thoracic hypaxial column. In the limb, their axons appear to choose paths and muscles at random.

scenes.tts: Inside the limb column comes one more choice. Lateral cells make Lim one, and their axons go dorsal.
scenes.caption: Inside the limb column comes one more choice. Lateral cells make Lim1, and their axons go dorsal.
scenes.visual: Zoom into the LMC: lateral cells labelled Lim1 send axons to the dorsal half of the limb.
scenes.narration: Inside the limb column comes one more choice. Lateral cells make Lim1, and their axons go dorsal.

scenes.tts: Medial cells keep Islet one, and their axons go ventral. Without Lim one, lateral axons lose their dorsal preference.
scenes.caption: Medial cells keep Isl1, and their axons go ventral. Without Lim1, lateral axons lose their dorsal preference.
scenes.visual: Medial cells labelled Isl1 send axons ventrally. Then Lim1 is crossed out and the lateral axons split at random. Credit: Kania, Johnson and Jessell, 2000.
scenes.narration: Medial cells keep Isl1, and their axons go ventral. Without Lim1, lateral axons lose their dorsal preference.

scenes.tts: Eph receptors and ephrins help carry out this choice, alongside other guidance systems.
scenes.visual: Eph receptors on the growth cones and ephrins in the limb mesenchyme, shown where the axons split, before they branch. Then an axon reaches a muscle. Pointer: see the neurotrophic hypothesis lesson.
scenes.narration: Eph receptors and ephrins help carry out this choice, alongside other guidance systems.

scenes.tts: Run these layers forward, and you have a recipe. Retinoic acid gives mouse stem cells a spinal character.
scenes.visual: A dish timeline: mouse embryonic stem cells, then retinoic acid added. Label: spinal character.
scenes.narration: Run these layers forward, and you have a recipe. Retinoic acid gives mouse stem cells a spinal character.

scenes.tts: A Hedgehog agonist pushes them toward the motor neuron domain. Then motor neurons appear.
scenes.visual: The timeline continues: Hedgehog agonist added, then Mnx1-positive motor neurons appear. Credit: Wichterle et al., 2002.
scenes.narration: A Hedgehog agonist pushes them toward the motor neuron domain. Then motor neurons appear.

scenes.tts: Put into an embryo, they reach muscle. But this recipe gives mostly medial column cells. One named pool is still hard to make.
scenes.visual: Inset: a transplanted motor neuron grows an axon to a muscle. Label on the dish: mostly MMC. Then a single muscle highlighted with a question mark: one named pool?
scenes.narration: Put into an embryo, they reach muscle. But this recipe gives mostly medial column cells. One named pool is still hard to make.

scenes.tts: Takeaway: overlapping layers set a motor neuron's class, its column, and its limb choice. Run them in order, and you have a recipe.
scenes.visual: Closing card: progenitor, code, column, limb choice drawn as overlapping bands, with Hox starting in the progenitor band. An arrow leads to a dish.
scenes.narration: Takeaway: overlapping layers set a motor neuron's class, its column, and its limb choice. Run them in order, and you have a recipe.
